case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court’s final judgment must be vacated after an appellate court later concludes that removal was improper because the district court wrongly dismissed the only nondiverse defendant, where that dismissal was interlocutory until it merged into the final judgment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332 (diversity jurisdiction), 1441–1447 (removal and remand), and the final-judgment/merger and interlocutory-revision principles reflected in Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that once the case reached a final federal judgment between completely diverse parties, that judgment should not be undone merely because the district court earlier made an erroneous interlocutory ruling dismissing a nondiverse party at the removal stage. They contend the Fifth Circuit’s rule creates waste and unfairness by requiring wholesale vacatur and state-court relitigation even when diversity exists at judgment, encourages strategic post-judgment forum shopping by plaintiffs, and undermines the stability and finality of federal judgments—especially where the federal court has already resolved dispositive issues (including gatekeeping of expert/scientific evidence).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue vacatur is required because the federal court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction from the start: removal was improper and the nondiverse-party dismissal that created diversity was itself erroneous and interlocutory, remaining subject to revision until it merged into final judgment. On that view, there was never a valid basis for federal adjudication, so the final judgment cannot stand. Respondents further contend petitioners’ proposed rule would let federal courts bootstrap jurisdiction through mistaken dismissals, weaken the statutory remand scheme, and improperly insulate jurisdictional errors from correction on appeal.
key_precedents: DiCenzo v. A-Best Prods. Co., 897 N.E.2d 132 (Ohio 2008)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest point on the other side remains my own initial instinct from Caterpillar: that we should look to complete diversity at final judgment and avoid undoing a fully litigated federal case for reasons of finality and efficiency. But Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s bootstrapping critique persuades me that Caterpillar’s premise is a legally effective, durable cure of the defect (e.g., a valid dismissal/settlement), whereas an interlocutory dismissal that remains revisable under Rule 54(b) and is later deemed erroneous cannot serve as the jurisdiction-conferring event without letting merits error manufacture jurisdiction. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand command reinforces that we cannot treat a reversible merits ruling as a “jurisdictional fact” that satisfies Congress’s removal scheme in §§ 1441–1447. Under a minimalist approach protective of institutional legitimacy, the narrower course is to vacate and remand rather than extend Caterpillar into a broader doctrine that risks jurisdiction-by-error.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument is the Chief’s Caterpillar-based finality principle—look only to whether diversity existed at final judgment—but that reading cannot overcome the mandatory text of § 1447(c) (“shall be remanded”) when jurisdiction is lacking as a matter of law, not merely as a momentary snapshot. Justice Barrett correctly identifies Caterpillar’s limiting premise: the defect must be cured by a legally effective, durable change in party posture; an interlocutory dismissal that remains revisable under Rule 54(b) and is later held erroneous cannot supply the jurisdictional “cure” Congress requires in §§ 1332 and 1441–1447. Justice Gorsuch’s bootstrapping concern is decisive under an originalist/textualist approach: allowing a reversible merits error to manufacture diversity expands federal jurisdiction beyond statutory authorization. Efficiency and finality are not sources of jurisdiction, so the judgment must be vacated and the case remanded.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point, pressed by the Chief, is Caterpillar’s final-judgment/efficiency principle—if diversity existed at judgment, we should not unwind a fully litigated case. But as Justice Barrett explains, Caterpillar’s rationale depends on a legally effective cure of the defect (a durable change in party posture), whereas here “diversity” exists only because of an interlocutory dismissal that Rule 54(b) makes revisable and that the court of appeals held erroneous, so the supposed jurisdictional cure was never lawful in the sense Congress required. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand once jurisdiction is lacking reinforces that we cannot treat a merits error as a jurisdiction-creating fact without bootstrapping federal power beyond §§ 1332 and 1441–1447. Practical finality concerns are real, but under a textualist, separation-of-powers view of jurisdiction, they cannot override the statutory limits on removal jurisdiction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point—Chief Justice Roberts’s Caterpillar-based finality argument—cannot carry the day because Caterpillar presupposes a legally effective cure of the jurisdictional defect, not “diversity” manufactured by a reversible interlocutory merits ruling. As Justice Barrett explains, Rule 54(b)’s revisability and the merger principle mean the dismissal never supplied a durable, congressionally recognized basis for § 1332 jurisdiction; once the court of appeals deems the dismissal erroneous, the supposed cure collapses. Justice Kagan’s framing is persuasive to me: treating that mistaken dismissal as a jurisdictional “fact” would bootstrap federal power beyond §§ 1441–1447 and, in real-world terms, undercut plaintiffs’ legitimate forum choice—often harming less powerful litigants—despite § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand command. Efficiency and finality are important, but they cannot override statutory limits on jurisdiction or sanitize a removal that was never authorized.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest opposing point remains the Chief’s Caterpillar finality frame—look only to diversity at final judgment and avoid undoing a completed federal case—but that works only if the jurisdictional defect was cured by a legally durable change in party posture. As Justice Barrett emphasizes, Rule 54(b)’s revisability and merger principles mean an interlocutory dismissal later held erroneous cannot supply a stable jurisdictional predicate; treating it as “curing” diversity would let a merits error manufacture the jurisdictional fact, effectively enlarging § 1332 and the removal/remand scheme. Justice Thomas’s focus on § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand command reinforces that efficiency cannot override the statute once the corrected legal picture shows complete diversity never lawfully existed. I therefore would vacate and remand rather than extend Caterpillar beyond its narrow premise.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest point on the other side—pressed by the Chief—is Caterpillar’s finality principle: if complete diversity exists at judgment, we should not unwind years of federal litigation. But as Justice Barrett explains, Caterpillar’s premise is a legally effective cure; here, “diversity” exists only because of an interlocutory dismissal that Rule 54(b) renders revisable and that the court of appeals has deemed erroneous, so the supposed cure never lawfully altered party posture. Justice Thomas’s statutory anchor reinforces the point: § 1447(c) says the case “shall be remanded” when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, and efficiency cannot convert a reversible merits error into jurisdiction Congress did not confer under §§ 1332 and 1441–1447. Treating an unlawful dismissal as a jurisdictional “fact” at judgment would be bootstrapping inconsistent with a textualist, separation-of-powers approach to federal jurisdiction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is the Chief’s Caterpillar finality argument—look only to complete diversity at final judgment and avoid unraveling a fully litigated case—but that presupposes a legally effective cure, not a snapshot produced by a reversible interlocutory error. Justice Barrett’s Rule 54(b)/merger point is decisive for me: because the dismissal was inherently revisable and later held erroneous, it cannot supply the kind of stable, jurisdiction-curing change in party posture that Caterpillar contemplated (as Grupo Dataflux cautions against expanding). Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch correctly anchor this in the statutory scheme—§ 1447(c) makes remand mandatory when jurisdiction is lacking, and efficiency cannot authorize jurisdiction Congress did not confer. Institutional concerns about finality matter, but extending Caterpillar to validate jurisdiction manufactured by mistake would undermine legitimacy by inviting jurisdiction-by-error.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest opposing point, pressed by the Chief (Roberts), is Caterpillar’s finality principle—looking only to whether diversity existed at final judgment even if removal was initially defective. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, Caterpillar presupposes a legally effective cure (a durable change in party posture), whereas here “diversity” existed only because of an interlocutory dismissal that Rule 54(b) treats as revisable and that the court of appeals later held erroneous, meaning the supposed cure was never lawful in the sense §§ 1332 and 1441–1447 require. Under the text of § 1447(c), once it is apparent that subject-matter jurisdiction was lacking, remand is mandatory; efficiency and finality cannot authorize jurisdiction manufactured by reversible merits error. I therefore would not extend Caterpillar in a way that bootstraps federal power from a mistaken dismissal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is the Chief’s Caterpillar-based finality argument—looking only to whether diversity existed at final judgment—but Justice Barrett persuasively identifies why that principle doesn’t travel here: the only “cure” was an interlocutory dismissal that Rule 54(b) makes revisable and that the court of appeals has now held legally erroneous, so it was never a legally durable jurisdiction-conferring change in party posture. As Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, letting a reversible merits mistake manufacture diversity would bootstrap federal jurisdiction beyond what §§ 1332 and 1441–1447 authorize and would dilute § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand command once the absence of jurisdiction is revealed. Under a procedural-fairness and practical-consequences lens, petitioner’s rule would incentivize jurisdiction-by-error and unfairly erode plaintiffs’ chosen forum, while Caterpillar’s narrow finality rationale is better read to apply only when the jurisdictional defect is actually and lawfully cured. I therefore remain with respondent and would vacate and remand rather than extend Caterpillar in a way that turns an appellate correction into a retroactive authorization of federal power.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), an erroneous failure to remand after improper removal does not require vacatur where complete diversity exists by the time final judgment is entered, because “finality, efficiency, and economy” weigh heavily against undoing a fully litigated federal judgment. Here, even if the district court’s dismissal of the lone nondiverse defendant was an interlocutory error subject to revision under Rule 54(b)’s interlocutory-revision principle, the jurisdictional inquiry at the moment of final judgment is what matters for whether that judgment must be set aside, and § 1332’s complete-diversity requirement was satisfied then. A rule of automatic vacatur would needlessly disrupt reliance interests and institutional legitimacy by requiring relitigation in state court despite a jurisdictionally proper posture at judgment, contrary to Caterpillar’s pragmatic, narrow exception to § 1447’s remand regime. Federalism concerns are adequately respected by recognizing the removal error but declining to unwind the final judgment absent an ongoing jurisdictional defect at the time of judgment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441–1447, removal is proper only when the district court has subject-matter jurisdiction, and § 1447(c) commands remand when it does not. If the sole basis for diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 was an erroneous, interlocutory dismissal of the only nondiverse defendant—one that remained revisable under the interlocutory principles reflected in Rule 54(b) until it merged into final judgment—then complete diversity never validly existed and the federal court lacked jurisdiction to enter judgment. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis preserves a final judgment only when the jurisdictional defect is actually cured before judgment (there, by a voluntary dismissal/settlement of the nondiverse party), not when “diversity” is manufactured by a mistaken dismissal that the court of appeals later determines should never have occurred. A judgment entered without subject-matter jurisdiction must be vacated notwithstanding efficiency concerns, because federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction fixed by the Constitution’s original meaning and Congress’s statutes, not equitable notions of finality.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332 and 1441–1447, a federal court must have subject-matter jurisdiction when it enters final judgment; if the only path to diversity was an interlocutory dismissal later deemed erroneous (and thus not a valid jurisdiction-curing event), the jurisdictional defect remained uncured at judgment and vacatur is required. Caterpillar permits affirmance only where the removal defect was statutory and the jurisdictional defect was actually cured before judgment by a legitimate event (there, a voluntary settlement and dismissal of the nondiverse party), not where diversity exists only because the district court wrongly eliminated the nondiverse defendant. Rule 54(b)’s interlocutory-revision/merger principles reinforce that the dismissal lacked finality until judgment, so on appeal its correction means the district court never had a proper jurisdictional basis to adjudicate the case to final judgment. Practical concerns about efficiency cannot override the limited-jurisdiction mandate and the remand scheme Congress established in § 1447.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Where the only basis for federal jurisdiction (complete diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1332) depended on an interlocutory dismissal of the sole nondiverse defendant that the court of appeals later determines was erroneous, diversity was never properly “cured” before judgment, and § 1447(c) requires remand once the absence of subject-matter jurisdiction is revealed. Caterpillar holds that an improper removal may be forgiven only when the jurisdictional defect is actually cured before final judgment; it also makes clear that if the defect “remains uncured, the judgment must be vacated.” Allowing a final judgment to stand here would effectively let a mistaken interlocutory merits ruling bootstrap federal jurisdiction, undermining the statutory limits on removal in §§ 1441–1447 and disadvantaging plaintiffs—often including vulnerable litigants—who are entitled to the forum they chose when federal jurisdiction is absent. The pragmatic costs of relitigation cannot override the constitutional and statutory command that federal courts may not adjudicate cases outside their limited jurisdiction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis permits affirmance after an improper removal only when the jurisdictional defect has been cured before final judgment; it emphasizes that a federal judgment cannot stand if subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking at the time of judgment. Here, the only basis for complete diversity at judgment was the district court’s erroneous dismissal of the sole nondiverse defendant—an interlocutory order that, under Rule 54(b) principles and the merger doctrine, remained revisable and is undone once the appellate court concludes it was wrong. Because that means the nondiverse party should have remained in the case, diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 was not properly established, and the removal/remand scheme in §§ 1441–1447 cannot be satisfied by “bootstrapping” jurisdiction through an incorrect dismissal. Workability and finality concerns are real, but they cannot override the statutory limits on jurisdiction when the defect is not genuinely cured (as in Caterpillar) and instead persists through an erroneous merits/jurisdictional ruling.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332 and 1441–1447, federal courts must have subject-matter jurisdiction, and if complete diversity is absent at the time of final judgment the judgment cannot stand. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis permits affirmance only when the jurisdictional defect existing at removal is cured before judgment; here, the only reason diversity existed at judgment was an erroneous, interlocutory dismissal of the sole nondiverse defendant—meaning the defect was never properly cured and cannot be bootstrapped by a mistaken merits ruling. Rule 54(b)’s interlocutory-revision/merger principles confirm the dismissal remained nonfinal and subject to correction, so the court of appeals properly treated the case as lacking a valid jurisdictional basis and required vacatur. Separation-of-powers principles counsel strict adherence to Congress’s jurisdictional limits and the remand scheme rather than judicially created finality exceptions beyond Caterpillar’s narrow cure rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332 and 1441–1447, the federal court must have subject-matter jurisdiction, and if complete diversity is absent at the time final judgment is entered, the judgment cannot stand. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), preserves a final judgment only when the initial removal defect is cured before judgment—there, diversity became complete when the nondiverse defendant was actually dismissed prior to trial. Here, because the only basis for diversity was an interlocutory dismissal later deemed erroneous (and thus not a valid cure, given Rule 54(b)’s interlocutory-revision/merger principles), the jurisdictional defect remained uncured through entry of final judgment, requiring vacatur and remand. That approach also respects the statutory remand scheme and judicial restraint by preventing jurisdiction from being “bootstrapped” through mistaken party dismissals.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1332 and 1441–1447, the district court may enter final judgment only if subject-matter jurisdiction exists at the time of judgment; if removal was improper and the only basis for diversity was an erroneous dismissal of the sole nondiverse defendant, that defect is not “cured” in any meaningful sense. Because the dismissal remained interlocutory under the principles reflected in Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b) until it merged into final judgment, the case proceeded to judgment on a jurisdictional premise that was legally wrong, and the final judgment cannot stand. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis allows a narrow, pragmatic exception when the jurisdictional defect is actually cured before judgment (there by voluntary settlement and dismissal), but it also makes clear that “if, at the end of the day and case, a jurisdictional defect remains uncured, the judgment must be vacated.” That understanding is consistent with this Court’s insistence that statutory limits on federal jurisdiction are not subject to equitable salvage once the defect persists through judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The removal statutes and § 1447(c) make remand mandatory once the district court determines (or should have determined) that subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, and an erroneous interlocutory dismissal of the sole nondiverse defendant cannot bootstrap federal jurisdiction where none properly existed. Caterpillar v. Lewis allows a final judgment to stand only when the jurisdictional defect is actually cured before judgment through a valid change in party alignment; it does not bless curing diversity through an interlocutory, reversible mistake that remains subject to revision under Rule 54(b) until it merges into final judgment. Consistent with Grupo Dataflux’s narrowing of Caterpillar, finality and efficiency concerns cannot override the requirement that federal courts act within their jurisdiction, particularly where the plaintiff preserved the jurisdictional objection. Vacatur and remand best protect procedural fairness and Congress’s remand scheme, avoiding incentives for federal courts to proceed on defective jurisdictional foundations.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court’s final judgment between completely diverse parties must be vacated after an appellate court later concludes that removal was improper because the district court erroneously dismissed the only nondiverse defendant at the time of removal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1332 (diversity jurisdiction); 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441 & 1447 (removal and remand); 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (final-judgment rule) (and related finality/merger principles in federal appellate procedure).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that once the case has proceeded to a final federal judgment between completely diverse parties, that judgment should not be undone simply because a removal-stage ruling (dismissing the nondiverse defendant) is later deemed erroneous. They contend the Fifth Circuit’s approach mandates automatic vacatur and remand even after full federal adjudication, undermining finality, wasting judicial resources, and enabling post-judgment “vertical forum shopping” (a plaintiff can relitigate in state court after losing on the merits in federal court). Petitioners maintain that the proper course is to preserve the federal judgment (or treat the removal error as cured/harmless once complete diversity exists at judgment), consistent with doctrines favoring finality and efficiency and Supreme Court precedent that resists unwinding completed federal proceedings for certain jurisdictional/removal defects when diversity exists by the time of judgment.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that because the district court’s dismissal of the nondiverse party at removal was interlocutory and remained subject to revision until final judgment (then merged into that judgment), the appellate court’s later conclusion that the dismissal was wrong means the federal court lacked removal jurisdiction when it proceeded. Under their view, the absence of proper subject-matter jurisdiction at the time the federal court adjudicated requires vacatur of the final judgment and remand; otherwise federal courts would be allowed to decide cases that belonged in state court, contrary to the removal statutes’ limits and the requirement that federal jurisdiction be secure. Respondents and supporting amici emphasize that plaintiffs are entitled to the forum Congress prescribed, and that preserving a federal merits loss entered after improper removal would improperly reward jurisdictional error and dilute statutory remand protections.
key_precedents: Grupo Dataflux v. Atlas Global Group, L.P., 541 U.S. 567 (2004)
American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Finn, 341 U.S. 6 (1951)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that an erroneous dismissal should not be treated as a “cure,” and that § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand language reflects Congress’s insistence that cases lacking diversity not be kept in federal court. But § 1447(c) is textually keyed to what the district court must do “before final judgment,” and it does not clearly prescribe a post-judgment nullification rule once complete diversity exists among the parties to the judgment; on that remedial question Caterpillar, as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito stress, treats the removal defect as antecedent and protects finality when jurisdiction exists “at the end of the day.” Finn is distinguishable because the jurisdictional defect persisted through judgment there, and Grupo Dataflux’s time-of-filing rule for original jurisdiction does not compel vacatur of a removed-case judgment where the only asserted error is an interlocutory dismissal that can be corrected through ordinary appellate review rather than retroactive jurisdictional collapse. Under a minimalist, legitimacy-protecting approach, I would preserve the judgment in the narrow circumstance where diversity at final judgment is undisputed and the remedy for any erroneous dismissal runs through merits/joinder correction, not automatic remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press that Caterpillar treats the problem as an antecedent removal defect once complete diversity exists at final judgment, and that § 1447(c) is not a post-judgment nullification rule. But that framing assumes the dismissal producing diversity was legally valid; if the dismissal was erroneous and the nondiverse party must be reinstated, then diversity was never lawfully cured and the district court lacked the adjudicatory power Congress withheld, making Finn’s core principle—no binding merits judgment from an improper removal—control. Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s finality concerns cannot override the statutory structure: § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand rule reflects a nonwaivable limit on federal jurisdiction, and Grupo Dataflux underscores that jurisdiction cannot be manufactured by later events or efficiency arguments. Newman-Green (as Justice Barrett invokes it) is inapposite because appellate severance of a dispensable party to perfect jurisdiction is categorically different from crediting an unlawful dismissal that wrongly erased a nondiverse party and thereby created the appearance of diversity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point: that an erroneous dismissal means diversity was never “legitimately” cured, so § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand language must control. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch explain, § 1447(c) is framed as an instruction to the district court “before final judgment” when it appears jurisdiction is lacking; it does not clearly create a post-judgment nullification rule that retroactively voids a merits judgment entered when the parties to that judgment are, in fact, completely diverse. Finn and Grupo Dataflux underscore that we cannot sustain a judgment entered without jurisdiction at the time of judgment, yet they do not answer Caterpillar’s remedial distinction for removed cases where the only defect is an antecedent removal-stage error that no longer exists “at the end of the day.” Treating every later-determined dismissal error as retroactively collapsing jurisdiction would sacrifice finality and impose heavy systemic costs without a clear textual command—especially given the availability of ordinary appellate correction of the dismissal itself.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest point that Caterpillar treats many removal defects as antecedent errors and protects finality once complete diversity exists at final judgment, and that § 1447(c) is framed as a pre-judgment instruction. But that remedial principle depends on a lawful cure; where diversity exists only because of an interlocutory dismissal later deemed erroneous, the federal court’s judgment rests on excluding a party who should have remained, so this is not merely a procedural “irregularity” but a jurisdictional failure Congress made nonwaivable. Justice Barrett’s Newman-Green analogy does not persuade me because appellate severance of a dispensable party is a permissible jurisdiction-perfection tool, not a license to treat an unlawful merits dismissal as curing jurisdiction after the fact—especially in light of Finn’s warning against allowing improper removal to ripen into a binding merits judgment. Under my pragmatic, access-to-justice lens, preserving such judgments would systematically dilute plaintiffs’ forum choice and invite removal-and-dismissal tactics, so vacatur and remand remain the only remedy that meaningfully enforces § 1447(c).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that § 1447(c)’s “shall be remanded” language cannot be evaded by calling an erroneous dismissal a “cure,” but that reading stretches § 1447(c) into a post-judgment vacatur command it does not textually supply—its trigger is what “appears” before final judgment and its remedy is directed to the district court in the moment. As the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Caterpillar’s operative distinction is remedial: when complete diversity exists among the parties to the final judgment, the earlier removal defect is best treated as an antecedent statutory/joinder error, not a continuing absence of adjudicatory power that automatically voids everything that follows. Finn and Grupo Dataflux do important work when jurisdiction is absent at judgment (or cannot be manufactured by later citizenship change), but they do not clearly govern a removed case where § 1332 is satisfied at judgment and the asserted mistake is an interlocutory dismissal reviewable on ordinary appellate grounds. I therefore would preserve the federal merits judgment while allowing appellate correction of the dismissal error, rather than converting that error into retroactive jurisdictional collapse.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is the statutory imperative in § 1447(c)—a case “shall be remanded” when jurisdiction is lacking—and his contention that an erroneous dismissal cannot “cure” diversity, so Finn would require vacatur. But § 1447(c) by its terms governs what the district court must do “before final judgment” when it “appears” jurisdiction is absent; it does not speak in post-judgment nullification terms, and I agree with the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett that reading it as an automatic unwind rule after a final merits judgment lacks a clear textual hook. Caterpillar supplies the governing remedial rule for removed cases: once complete diversity exists among the parties to the judgment, the earlier removal-stage defect is not treated as a continuing absence of adjudicatory power at judgment, and any error in dismissing the nondiverse party is addressed through ordinary appellate correction rather than retroactive jurisdictional collapse. Grupo Dataflux and Finn remain distinguishable on their face because they involved judgments entered when jurisdiction was absent at judgment, whereas here jurisdiction exists at the time the federal court entered final judgment on the parties then properly before it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas offers the strongest objection: if the nondiverse defendant was wrongly dismissed, then diversity was never legitimately cured and § 1447(c) plus Finn should compel vacatur and remand. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, Caterpillar’s operative move is remedial and finality-based: once complete diversity indisputably exists among the parties to the judgment, the case no longer suffers from an uncured jurisdictional defect at judgment, and § 1447(c)’s “before final judgment” command does not clearly translate into a post-judgment nullification rule. Grupo Dataflux underscores the time-of-filing rule in original jurisdiction and confirms we cannot sustain judgments entered without jurisdiction at judgment, yet it preserves Caterpillar’s removed-case distinction where jurisdiction exists “at the end of the day.” Under an institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, I would treat any erroneous dismissal as an ordinary appealable party/merits error, not as retroactively voiding the federal court’s adjudicatory power and unraveling a completed merits judgment absent a clearer statutory directive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s objection—that § 1447(c)’s “shall be remanded” language compels vacatur if the nondiverse defendant was wrongly dismissed—squarely targets the statutory text, but it still reads § 1447(c) as a post-judgment nullification rule rather than a directive to the district court while the case is pending (“before final judgment”). As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Caterpillar’s controlling distinction is remedial: where the parties to the final judgment are in fact completely diverse, the antecedent removal-stage defect does not necessarily negate adjudicatory power at the moment of judgment, and Congress has not clearly required automatic unwinding of a completed merits judgment in that circumstance. Finn and Grupo Dataflux, invoked by Justice Sotomayor, remain distinguishable because they involve jurisdictional absence at judgment or uncured time-of-filing problems, whereas here the asserted mistake is best treated as an appealable merits/joinder error (with ordinary corrective relief) rather than retroactive destruction of subject-matter jurisdiction. On a textualist reading attentive to both § 1447(c)’s temporal phrasing and our precedent, I would affirm.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is that § 1447(c) speaks pre-judgment and Caterpillar treats some removal defects as antecedent “irregularities,” protecting finality once diversity exists at judgment. But that framing collapses where, as Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, the only way diversity “appears” at judgment is through an erroneous dismissal later determined to be legally wrong—meaning the supposed cure is not a lawful party-structure at all, and the federal court’s exercise of power rests on stripping a party Congress’s jurisdictional scheme required to remain. Justice Barrett’s Newman-Green analogy doesn’t undermine that conclusion because it involves a permissible severance of a dispensable party to perfect jurisdiction, not insulating a merits-error dismissal that defeats the plaintiff’s statutory entitlement to remand when jurisdiction is lacking. Pragmatically, treating erroneous dismissals as adequate “cures” incentivizes removal-and-dismissal maneuvering and dilutes the nonwaivable nature of subject-matter limits, so vacatur and remand remain the proper remedy notwithstanding the finality costs flagged by Justice Alito.

John Roberts.reasoning: Following Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), once complete diversity indisputably exists by the time of final judgment, the interests of finality and judicial economy generally counsel against vacating a merits judgment solely for an antecedent removal error under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441 and 1447. Here, the asserted defect stems from an erroneous dismissal decision at the removal stage, but by the time judgment entered the federal court had jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332, making automatic vacatur an unnecessarily disruptive remedy that invites strategic relitigation and undermines the stability of final judgments under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. Finn and Grupo Dataflux underscore the centrality of jurisdiction, but they do not compel setting aside a fully litigated federal judgment where diversity is present at judgment and the remaining error is best addressed on ordinary appellate merits grounds rather than through jurisdictional nullification. A narrow rule preserving the final judgment in these circumstances best protects institutional legitimacy while respecting Congress’s jurisdictional limits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The removal statutes impose a mandatory duty to remand when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, see 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c), and a federal court may not enter a binding merits judgment without jurisdiction conferred by 28 U.S.C. § 1332. Caterpillar held only that an improper removal does not require vacatur when the jurisdictional defect (lack of complete diversity) is actually cured before final judgment, 519 U.S. at 76–77; it did not authorize a district court to "cure" jurisdiction through an erroneous dismissal that is later determined to have been improper. Because the nondiverse defendant should have remained in the case, complete diversity was not truly present when the federal court proceeded, so the final judgment must be vacated and the case remanded consistent with § 1447(c) and Finn’s insistence that federal courts not retain judgments entered without proper jurisdictional footing.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Once the case reached a final federal judgment between completely diverse parties, the Article III and § 1332 requirements for subject-matter jurisdiction were satisfied, and the remaining problem is best understood as a statutory removal irregularity under §§ 1441 and 1447. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis held that where complete diversity exists by the time of judgment, “considerations of finality, efficiency, and economy” can outweigh the earlier removal-stage defect, and vacating a fully litigated merits judgment would waste resources and invite forum manipulation. Unlike American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Finn, this is not a situation where federal jurisdiction was absent at judgment; and Grupo Dataflux’s time-of-filing rule does not justify undoing a completed federal adjudication where diversity is present at judgment in a removed case. Textually, §§ 1447(c) and (d) are aimed at prompt remand, not post-judgment nullification after jurisdiction is secure, so the judgment should stand.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Because removal jurisdiction must be proper under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441 and 1447, an erroneous involuntary dismissal of the only nondiverse defendant at the time of removal means the federal court proceeded without statutory authority to adjudicate the case, and the error merges into the final judgment under § 1291. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis preserves a final judgment only where the jurisdictional defect is cured before judgment by the voluntary elimination of the diversity-destroying party; here, the later conclusion that the dismissal was wrong means the defect was never legitimately cured. Grupo Dataflux confirms that efficiency and finality do not themselves “cure” a jurisdictional defect, and Finn underscores that judgments entered after an improper removal should be vacated to respect Congress’s limits on federal jurisdiction. Vacatur and remand best protect litigants—especially vulnerable plaintiffs—from being forced into an unauthorized federal forum and preserves the statutory remand entitlement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis teaches that when a case ends in a final federal judgment between completely diverse parties, an earlier removal defect need not require vacatur so long as no jurisdictional defect remains “at the end of the day and case,” reflecting the practical balance Congress struck in 28 U.S.C. §§ 1441 and 1447. Here, by final judgment the parties were completely diverse under 28 U.S.C. § 1332, and unwinding the merits judgment would needlessly sacrifice finality protected by 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and invite wasteful relitigation after full federal adjudication. Unlike American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Finn—where the federal court never had diversity jurisdiction to support the judgment—this case culminated in a diversity-satisfying alignment, making the error at removal stage effectively non-dispositive at the point of judgment. Grupo Dataflux limits “cure” where diversity is manufactured by post-filing citizenship changes, but it preserves Caterpillar’s core point that a removal-stage defect does not mandate vacatur once complete diversity exists at judgment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The removal statutes (§§ 1441, 1447) regulate the path a case takes into federal court, but they do not require automatic vacatur of a merits judgment where, by the time final judgment entered, the parties were completely diverse under § 1332 and the district court possessed subject-matter jurisdiction in the case’s final posture. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis holds that even when removal was erroneous, a final judgment need not be unwound once the jurisdictional defect has been cured before judgment, emphasizing “finality, efficiency, and economy” and warning against the “exorbitant cost” of postjudgment vacatur and remand. That approach respects the separation of powers by applying the statutes as written (no postjudgment vacatur command) while honoring Article III’s jurisdictional limits at the time of judgment, and it avoids incentivizing postjudgment forum manipulation. To the extent ambiguity remains about the consequence of an initial removal defect after complete diversity exists at judgment, Caterpillar’s finality rule supplies the controlling answer rather than expanding § 1447 beyond its text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), an improper-removal defect based on incomplete diversity at the time of removal does not compel vacatur where complete diversity exists by the time of final judgment and the case has been fully adjudicated in federal court. Here, even if the district court erred in dismissing the only nondiverse defendant at removal, once the final judgment is between completely diverse parties and no Article III/§ 1332 defect remains at judgment, the strong practical interests in finality and workability counsel against automatic vacatur and remand, consistent with Caterpillar’s emphasis on avoiding wasted judicial resources. Grupo Dataflux limits Caterpillar’s reach when diversity is lacking at final judgment, but it preserves Caterpillar’s core holding that a cured diversity defect does not require undoing a completed federal proceeding. Reading §§ 1441 and 1447 to mandate vacatur after merits judgment would invite inefficient relitigation and undermine the final-judgment rule in § 1291 without a clear statutory command.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1332’s requirement of complete diversity is a subject-matter jurisdiction prerequisite, but Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), teaches that when complete diversity exists by the time of final judgment, a prior removal defect under §§ 1441–1447 does not require automatic vacatur given the strong finality and efficiency interests embedded in § 1291’s final-judgment regime. Here, although the district court erred in dismissing the nondiverse defendant at the time of removal, the relevant question at the “end of the day” is whether a jurisdictional defect remained uncured at judgment; if judgment was entered between completely diverse parties, Caterpillar counsels affirmance rather than unwinding completed federal proceedings. That approach is methodologically consistent with Newman-Green, Inc. v. Alfonzo-Larrain, 490 U.S. 826 (1989), which permits curing diversity defects to preserve judgments, while respecting Grupo Dataflux, 541 U.S. 567 (2004), as a narrower bar on post-filing changes to party citizenship rather than post-removal curing by party dismissal. Reading the removal statutes textually, § 1447(c)’s remand command operates when the case “appears” to lack subject-matter jurisdiction while the action is pending; once final judgment has been entered with § 1332 jurisdiction satisfied, the remedy is not mandatory vacatur absent an uncured jurisdictional defect at judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1447(c) requires remand whenever it appears the district court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, and if the only nondiverse defendant was wrongly dismissed, complete diversity under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 was not satisfied when the federal court adjudicated the merits and entered final judgment. Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis allows a final judgment to stand only when the jurisdictional defect is cured before judgment; it simultaneously emphasizes that if a jurisdictional defect remains “uncured,” the judgment must be vacated, preserving the statutory limits Congress placed on removal under §§ 1441 and 1447. Because the erroneous dismissal here merges into the final judgment and the federal forum was never properly secured, vacatur and remand best vindicate procedural fairness and the plaintiff’s entitlement to the congressionally prescribed forum, notwithstanding efficiency concerns. This approach also respects the final-judgment rule in 28 U.S.C. § 1291 while enforcing the nonwaivable nature of subject-matter jurisdiction.
